detail:
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) Expands AI Infrastructure Cooling, Is The Stock Fully Priced?
Simply Wall St

AMD
Trade AMD on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) just deepened its AI infrastructure push through a collaboration with nVent to add rack-level liquid-assisted cooling to the Helios rackscale platform, bringing thermal design directly into the AI hardware story.

For shareholders, the recent news lands during a choppy stretch. AMD's share price has retreated over the past week, including a 1-day share price decline of 5.73%, even after a 30-day share price return of 13.21% and a very strong 3-year total shareholder return of 457.44% that still signals powerful long-term momentum.

Capitalize on the AI infrastructure momentum around Advanced Micro Devices by scanning a curated set of potential beneficiaries across 93 AI infrastructure stocks.

Advanced Micro Devices now trades about 8% below one intrinsic value estimate and roughly 11% below the average analyst target after a sharp pullback. Is that discount true mispricing, or is it simply breathing room in a hot AI story?

Most Popular Narrative: 37% Undervalued

Against AMD's last close at $570.82, the most followed narrative on Advanced Micro Devices argues for a fair value of $907.32, which implies a large gap that current pricing does not reflect according to that framework.

The market previously priced AMD as a "forced choice" spillover. Recent quarters, particularly the massive Data Center revenue run-rates achieved into 2026, have completely shattered this narrative. AMD is no longer just a GPU alternative; it has cemented itself as the definitive "End-to-End AI Platform." With hyperscalers aggressively expanding their infrastructure, AMD is rapidly scaling from a "Second Player" into the absolute backbone of modern AI data centers.

See why 194 investors see Advanced Micro Devices as 37% undervalued.

According to Talos, who authored the widely followed narrative, the implied upside rests on AMD reaching $232b of revenue by 2031 with a 32% profit margin and applying a future P/E of 30x. That path feeds into the $907.32 fair value estimate while using an 8% discount rate to bring those projected cash flows back to today in present value terms.

For context, that narrative leans heavily on AI infrastructure, with AMD's Data Center segment already generating $22.2b of the current $41.3b in annual revenue and earnings growth that reached 137.4% over the past year. Supporters of this view see the shift toward data center and embedded products as a key reason the market price, even after a strong 1-year total return of 143.36%, still sits below that long run valuation anchor.

What Happened?

A number of stocks fell in the morning session after hotter-than-expected inflation data compounded fears that elevated borrowing costs will curb artificial intelligence infrastructure spending.

The sell-off followed a Bureau of Labor Statistics release showing September wholesale prices climbed 1.3%, marking a 6.3% annual advance that outpaced the 5.5% projection from economists polled by Dow Jones. Compounding an above-forecast consumer price print from the prior session, the hotter CPI inflation reading drove the 10-year Treasury yield past 5.27%, based on CNBC market data. However, rates cooled off a bit in the pre market session.Higher benchmark rates threaten the debt-heavy funding required to power data center expansion. Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives observed in a client note carried by CNBC that while compute demand remains sound, climbing yields directly inflate project financing costs and intensify scrutiny on balance sheets.

Semiconductor valuations reflect aggressive, uninterrupted capital spending from cloud hyperscalers. When capital costs stay elevated, the payback timeline on multi-billion-dollar clusters lengthens, raising the hurdle rate for new hardware commitments and delaying order realization across the component supply chain.

The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.

Zooming In On FormFactor (FORM)

FormFactor's shares are extremely volatile and have had 78 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 3 days ago when the stock dropped 5.7% on the news that worries weighed on memory chipmakers and sparked selling pressure across the broader semiconductor sector, following news of domestic Chinese technological advancements and looming labor strikes in Taiwan.

Chip stocks slipped even as TSMC's third-quarter revenue rose 51% year over year, beating market forecasts.

Saxo said investor focus is shifting to whether companies can turn strong demand into sustainable cash flow and earnings growth.

The firm noted that yields on some CoreWeave bonds have approached 15%, which does not necessarily signal an imminent default.

Semiconductor and memory chip stocks extended their losing streak on Thursday as concerns over mounting debt and rising financing costs for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure projects continued to weigh on the sector.

Nvidia (NVDA) fell over 2%, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) dropped 4%, while Micron Technology (MU) and SanDisk (SNDK) slipped roughly 4% and 6%, respectively, extending losses from earlier in the week.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

In a Thursday note, Saxo Bank Chief Investment Strategist Charu Chanana said there was insufficient evidence of a systemic AI credit crisis, even as investors increasingly questioned the sustainability of the financing model behind the infrastructure boom.

Chip stocks' price performance month-to-date on Oct 15 as of 11:00 a.m. | Source: Koyfin
Saxo Warns AI Financing Squeeze Could Hit Chip Suppliers

However, Chanana warned that financing pressures in the AI infrastructure industry could eventually affect semiconductor suppliers if companies are forced to scale back investment.

The bank noted that infrastructure providers depend on financing and large customer contracts to fund expansion, while equipment suppliers rely on those customers continuing to build capacity.

If rising borrowing costs force infrastructure operators to moderate spending, Saxo said the impact could spread beyond chipmakers to industrial equipment, power infrastructure and construction companies.

Saxo pointed to AI cloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV), where yields on some bonds have approached 15%. Elevated bond yields do not necessarily signal an imminent default. However, repricing of CoreWeave's debt suggests that investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost, the note stated.

Record TSMC Earnings Fail To Halt Chip Selloff

The selling continued despite Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) reporting a strong quarter. The chip manufacturer's fiscal third-quarter (Q3) revenue rose 51% to NT$1.49 trillion, beating market forecasts. In dollar terms, sales rose 41%.

Early Thursday, TSM forecast fourth-quarter revenue would rise up to 61% from a year ago, after posting its sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings.

Tech sell-off rolls on as hot inflation data stokes rate worries

A rout in tech firms led heavy losses in Seoul (Jung Yeon-je)

Asian stocks plunged and the sell-off in tech stocks continued on Wall Street on Thursday as investors worried that forecast-topping US inflation data would force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again.

"A glance across major US equities this morning shows that the tech sell-off is still in progress," said market analyst David Morrison at Trade Nation.

"Once again, chip stocks are in the forefront of the current round of derisking," he added.

Shares in AI chip giant Nvidia shed 2.2 percent.

Those in rivals AMD and Marvell were both down around four percent in late morning New York trading.

Shares in AI data centre infrastructure company CoreWeave fell 3.6 percent after plunging 15.5 percent on Wednesday.

The company is a big client of Nvidia chips and Nvidia is a major shareholder.

The Nasdaq Composite, which has the heaviest exposure to tech stocks, shed 0.3 percent.

The blue-chip Dow rose, however.

"Rotation out of highly speculative AI infrastructure into established sectors helped the Dow gain over half a percentage point," said IG analyst Axel Rudolph.

European stock markets were more resilient, benefitting from their lower exposure to the tech sector.

Seoul and Tokyo bore the brunt of the selling in Asia as traders bailed out of chipmakers, tracking sharp losses on Wall Street on Wednesday.

Seoul's Kospi dived more than eight percent -- leading to a brief trading halt -- before slightly paring the losses, with semiconductor firm SK hynix sinking more than 11 percent and Samsung more than nine percent.

Tokyo shed close to five percent, driven by sharp falls for Advantest, Kioxia and investment titan SoftBank.

"The tech sell-off has continued with pace, exacerbated by US inflation data which increased expectations for US interest rate hikes this month," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

"US Treasury bond yields fell, suggesting that investors are moving into supposed lower-risk assets," he added.

Markets, already struggling with concerns about the outlook for the AI investment boom, were stung after data released on Wednesday showed the US consumer price index jumped more than expected to 3.7 percent in September.

Figures released on Thursday showed US wholesale inflation surged past analysts' expectations in September -- the 6.3 percent increase from one year ago -- marking its biggest year-on-year jump since 2022 as petrol prices rocketed due to the war with Iran.

The inflation figures put pressure on the Fed to raise rates at least once more following September's hike.
